claim: M proteins are the major surface-localized virulence factor of Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus or Strep A).
source: M proteins are the major surface-localized virulence factor of the widespread and potentially deadly bacterial pathogen Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus or Strep A) (Ghosh, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ghosh, 2018

claim: One of the primary functions of M proteins is to enable Strep A to evade human innate and adaptive immune responses.
source: One of the primary functions of M proteins is to enable Strep A to evade human innate and adaptive immune responses.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about M proteins

claim: M proteins enable Strep A to evade immune responses through interaction with select human proteins.
source: This is brought about by interaction of M proteins with select human proteins.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge

claim: Over 220 different M protein types have been identified.
source: M proteins are antigenically sequence variable, with over 220 different types having been identified (McMillan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to McMillan et al., 2013

claim: M proteins generally have a propensity to form dimeric, α-helical coiled coils.
source: Despite this variation, the primary sequences of M proteins generally have a propensity to form dimeric, α-helical coiled coils, as verified by direct experimental evidence (McNamara et al., 2008; Macheboeuf et al., 2011; Buffalo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: The propensity of M proteins to form coiled coils is distinguishable by the presence of heptad repeats.
source: This propensity is easily distinguishable by the presence of heptad repeats (Manjula and Fischetti, 1980), in which amino acids in the a and d positions of the heptad are usually small and hydrophobic, and form the hydrophobic core of the coiled coil.
evidence: Supported by citation to Manjula and Fischetti, 1980

claim: In heptad repeats, amino acids in the a and d positions are usually small and hydrophobic and form the hydrophobic core of the coiled coil.
source: This propensity is easily distinguishable by the presence of heptad repeats (Manjula and Fischetti, 1980), in which amino acids in the a and d positions of the heptad are usually small and hydrophobic, and form the hydrophobic core of the coiled coil.
evidence: Supported by citation and established knowledge of coiled coil structure

claim: LL-37 consists of a short amphipathic α-helix.
source: This is because LL-37 also has a simple topography: LL-37 consists of a short amphipathic α-helix.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of LL-37 structure

claim: LL-37 is a member of the cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide family.
source: LL-37 is a member of the cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide family and constitutes a major host immune defense against Strep A, as well as other pathogens (Nizet et al., 2001; LaRock et al., 2015; LaRock and Nizet, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: LL-37 constitutes a major host immune defense against Strep A and other pathogens.
source: LL-37 is a member of the cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide family and constitutes a major host immune defense against Strep A, as well as other pathogens (Nizet et al., 2001; LaRock et al., 2015; LaRock and Nizet, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nizet et al., 2001; LaRock et al., 2015; LaRock and Nizet, 2015

claim: LL-37 is a 37-amino acid peptide proteolytically generated from the precursor protein hCAP-18.
source: The 37-amino acid peptide is proteolytically generated from the precursor protein hCAP-18, which is produced by neutrophils, macrophages, mast cells, and keratinocytes, along with other epithelial cell types (Nizet et al., 2001; Zaiou et al., 2003; Wong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: hCAP-18 is produced by neutrophils, macrophages, mast cells, keratinocytes, and other epithelial cell types.
source: The 37-amino acid peptide is proteolytically generated from the precursor protein hCAP-18, which is produced by neutrophils, macrophages, mast cells, and keratinocytes, along with other epithelial cell types (Nizet et al., 2001; Zaiou et al., 2003; Wong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nizet et al., 2001; Zaiou et al., 2003; Wong et al., 2013

claim: LL-37 functions by inserting into and lysing bacterial plasma membranes.
source: Like other amphipathic α-helical antimicrobial peptides, LL-37 functions by inserting into and lysing bacterial plasma membranes (Sancho-Vaello et al., 2017; Sancho-Vaello et al., 2020; Schneider et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sancho-Vaello et al., 2017; Sancho-Vaello et al., 2020; Schneider et al., 2016

claim: M1 protein neutralizes the antimicrobial activity of LL-37 by sequestering it in a 'protein trap' on the Strep A surface.
source: Notably, M1 protein was shown to neutralize the antimicrobial activity of LL-37 by sequestering it in a 'protein trap' on the Strep A surface and away from its target of action, the bacterial membrane (LaRock et al., 2015, Lauth et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to LaRock et al., 2015 and Lauth et al., 2009

claim: M1 protein released in soluble form from the Strep A surface has LL-37 neutralization capacity.
source: Not only does M1 protein attached to bacterial surface have this neutralization capacity, but so too does M1 protein released in soluble form from the Strep A surface, as occurs during infection (LaRock et al., 2015; Herwald et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to LaRock et al., 2015; Herwald et al., 2004

claim: M1 protein binds the LL-37 precursor hCAP-18 and prevents the proteolytic generation of LL-37.
source: M1 protein also binds the LL-37 precursor hCAP-18 and consequently prevents the proteolytic generation of LL-37 (LaRock et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to LaRock et al., 2015

claim: M58N100 and M87N100 bind LL-37.
source: M58N100 and M87N100 bound LL-37, as did the M1HB fragment (Figure 1A), while the others did not bind LL-37 above background level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The level of LL-37 binding by M58N100, M87N100, and M1HB is approximately similar.
source: The level of LL-37 binding by M58N100, M87N100, and M1HB was approximately similar.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data in Figure 1A

claim: The KD for the M1/LL-37 complex is approximately 1 μM.
source: As a point of comparison, the KD for the M1/LL-37 complex is ~1 μM (LaRock and Nizet, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to LaRock and Nizet, 2015

claim: M58 and M87 proteins are the first M proteins besides M1 protein identified to bind LL-37.
source: To our knowledge, M58 and M87 proteins are the first M proteins besides M1 protein identified to bind LL-37.
evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge of the literature and their experimental findings

claim: M58N100 and M87N100 exogenously added to Δemm1 increased the LL-37 minimal inhibitory concentration.
source: Likewise, M58N100 or M87N100 exogenously added to Δemm1 increased the LL-37 minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC), and in this case, these effects were statistically significant and M87N100 had the greatest effect (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: M87N100 had the greatest effect in increasing LL-37 MIC among M58N100, M87N100, and M1HB.
source: Likewise, M58N100 or M87N100 exogenously added to Δemm1 increased the LL-37 minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC), and in this case, these effects were statistically significant and M87N100 had the greatest effect (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The structure of the GCN4-M87/LL-37 complex was determined to 2.1 Å resolution limit.
source: The structure of the GCN4-M87/LL-37 complex was determined through molecular replacement to 2.1 Å resolution limit (Table 1, Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data in Table 1 and figures

claim: GCN4-M87 binds and neutralizes LL-37.
source: The GCN4-M87 fusion protein was verified to bind and neutralize LL-37, as gauged by co-precipitation and MIC assays, respectively (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: GCN4-M87 bound LL-37 and led to a statistically significant increase in the LL-37 MIC, to an even greater extent than observed for M87N100.
source: GCN4-M87 bound LL-37 and led to a statistically significant increase in the LL-37 MIC, to an even greater extent than observed for M87N100.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: A single LL-37 molecule is bound to a dimer of GCN4-M87 in the crystal structure.
source: The structure revealed a single LL-37 molecule bound to a dimer of GCN4-M87 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Two nearly identical 1:2 complexes occupied the asymmetric unit of the GCN4-M87/LL-37 crystal.
source: Two nearly identical 1:2 complexes occupied the asymmetric unit of the crystal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, RMSD 0.70 Å).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Almost the entire length of LL-37 is visible in the crystal structure and is predominantly in α-helical conformation.
source: Almost the entire length of LL-37, which was predominantly in α-helical conformation, was visible in the crystal structure.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data

claim: In the GCN4-M87/LL-37 complex, only the GCN4 portion forms a coiled coil while the M87 α-helices are unfurled and asymmetrically disposed.
source: GCN4-M87 was likewise in α-helical conformation throughout, but strikingly, only the GCN4 portion formed a coiled coil while the M87 α-helices were unfurled and asymmetrically disposed.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2

claim: Free GCN4-M87 forms a dimeric coiled coil throughout.
source: Free GCN4-M87 formed a dimeric coiled coil throughout (Figure 2B), indicating that the unfurling of the M87 α-helices was unique to the bound form (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The unfurling of the M87 α-helices is unique to the bound form with LL-37.
source: Free GCN4-M87 formed a dimeric coiled coil throughout (Figure 2B), indicating that the unfurling of the M87 α-helices was unique to the bound form (Figure 2C).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of bound and free structures

claim: The greatest extent of unfurling in M87 occurs at Phe91, where the distance between Cα atoms is 8.7 Å in the free form but 15.6 Å in the bound form.
source: The greatest extent of unfurling occurred at Phe91, in which the distance between Cα atoms was 8.7 Å in the free form but 15.6 Å in the bound form.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data comparing free and bound structures

claim: Only the M87 portion of GCN4-M87 contacts LL-37.
source: Only the M87 portion contacted LL-37, and therefore we will refer only to M87 rather than GCN4-M87 hereafter.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data

claim: The two M87 α-helices and the LL-37 α-helix together form a parallel, three-helix bundle.
source: The two M87 α-helices and the LL-37 α-helix together formed a parallel, three-helix bundle.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data

claim: One M87 α-helix (M87α1) makes more contact with LL-37 (1016 Å2 total buried surface area) than the other (M87α2, 491 Å2).
source: One of the M87 α-helices made more contact with LL-37 (1016 Å2 total buried surface area, average of the two complexes in the asymmetric unit of the crystal) (Figure 3, dark blue) while the other made less but still substantial contact (491 Å2 average total buried surface area) (Figure 3, cyan)
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data and buried surface area calculations

claim: Hydrophobic interactions dominate the M87/LL-37 interaction interface.
source: Overall, hydrophobic interactions dominated the interaction site.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data showing the nature of contacts

claim: Hydrophobic M87 amino acids that occupied core a or d positions in the free form are exposed in the bound form and contact the hydrophobic face of LL-37.
source: Most notably, a number of hydrophobic M87 amino acids that occupied the core a or d positions and contacted each other in the free form, as is typical of coiled coils, were exposed in the bound form and instead contacted the hydrophobic face of the amphipathic LL-37 α-helix.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data comparing free and bound structures

claim: Nearly five helical turns of LL-37 (Phe5-Val21) and M87 protein (Leu74-Trp92) engage one another.
source: Nearly five helical turns of LL-37 (Phe5-Val21) and M87 protein (Leu74-Trp92) engaged one another.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data

claim: LL-37 Phe5 and Phe6 are surrounded by hydrophobic M87 amino acids Leu74, Ala77, and Tyr81 from M87α1 and Ala77 from M87α2.
source: Near the N-terminus of LL-37, a consecutive pair of phenylalanines, Phe5 and Phe6, was surrounded by hydrophobic a and d position amino acids of M87–Leu74 (a, usual position in heptad), Ala77 (d), and Tyr81 (a) from M87α along with Ala77 from M87α2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3A

claim: LL-37 Phe5, Phe6 and M87 Tyr81 form a series of π-stacks.
source: The two LL-37 Phe's and M87 Tyr81 formed a series of π-stacks.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data

claim: LL-37 Ile13 engages in a ring of isoleucines with M87 Ile84 from each M87 helix.
source: Two helical turns later in LL-37 was Ile13 that engaged in a ring of isoleucines, with M87 contributing Ile84 (d) from each of its helices (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3B

claim: LL-37 Phe17 packs against M87 Leu88 from each M87 helix and π-stacks against M87α2 Phe91.
source: A further helical turn later in LL-37 was Phe17 that packed against a pair of M87 leucines, Leu88 (a), one from each of the M87 helices, and π-stacked against M87α2 Phe91 (d) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3C

claim: LL-37 Ile20 is surrounded by M87α1 Phe91 and Trp92.
source: Lastly, one more helical turn further in LL-37 were Ile20, which was surrounded by M87α1 Phe91 (d) and Trp92
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3D

claim: LL-37 Val21 packs against M87α2 Phe91.
source: Val21, which packed against M87α2 Phe91
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3D

claim: LL-37 Arg23's aliphatic side-chain atoms pack against M87α1 Trp92.
source: and Arg23 whose aliphatic side-chain atoms packed against M87α1 Trp92 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3D

claim: LL-37 Ser9 forms a hydrogen bond with M87α1 Glu85.
source: These hydrophobic contacts were supplemented by a sparingly few polar ones, which occurred all within a small polar break in the hydrophobic face of LL-37, near its N-terminus: LL-37 Ser9 and Lys12 formed a hydrogen bond and salt bridge, respectively, with M87α1 Glu85 (Figure 3E)
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3E

claim: LL-37 Lys12 forms a salt bridge with M87α1 Glu85.
source: These hydrophobic contacts were supplemented by a sparingly few polar ones, which occurred all within a small polar break in the hydrophobic face of LL-37, near its N-terminus: LL-37 Ser9 and Lys12 formed a hydrogen bond and salt bridge, respectively, with M87α1 Glu85 (Figure 3E)
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3E

claim: In one of the two complexes in the asymmetric unit, LL-37 Lys12 also forms a salt bridge with M87α1 Glu89.
source: and in one of the two complexes, LL-37 Lys12 also formed a salt bridge with M87α1 Glu89.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data

claim: Dual alanine substitutions of M87 Tyr81 and Ile84 significantly decrease LL-37 interaction.
source: Dual alanine substitutions of M87 Tyr81 (a) and Ile84 (d), which interacted with LL-37 Phe5, Phe6, and Ile13 (Figure 3A and B), significantly decreased LL-37 interaction (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: M87 Y81A/I84A has a similar structure to wild-type M87 protein at 37°C.
source: M87 Y81A/I84A was verified through circular dichroism (CD) to have a similar structure to wild-type M87 protein at 37°C (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: M87 Y81A/I84A has a temperature-induced unfolding profile similar to wild-type M87 protein.
source: Additionally, M87 Y81A/I84A had a temperature-induced unfolding profile similar to that of wild-type M87 protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), also as monitored by CD.
evidence: Supported by CD melting curve data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Alanine substitutions of Tyr81 and Ile84 affect LL-37 binding directly rather than through compromised structure or stability.
source: These results indicated that alanine substitutions of Tyr81 and Ile84 affected LL-37 binding directly rather than indirectly through compromised structure, stability, or both.
evidence: Inferred from CD and binding data

claim: Alanine substitution of M87 Leu88 and Phe91 markedly decreases LL-37 interaction.
source: Alanine substitution of M87 Leu88 (a) and Phe91 (d), which interacted hydrophobically with LL-37 Phe17, Ile20, and Val21 (Figure 3C and D), likewise markedly decreased LL-37 interaction (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: M87 L88A/F91A has secondary structure and stability resembling wild-type M87 protein.
source: The secondary structure and stability of M87 L88A/F91A resembled that of wild-type M87 protein as well (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by CD data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Substitution of M87 Trp92 with alanine increases LL-37 interaction.
source: A substantial amount of the surface area of M87 Trp92 was buried by contact with LL-37, but surprisingly, substitution of this amino acid with alanine increased LL-37 interaction (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental mutagenesis data

claim: M87 W92R is almost entirely deficient in LL-37 interaction.
source: Indeed, M87 W92R was almost entirely deficient in LL-37 interaction (Figure 4A and B), while showing no changes in secondary structure or stability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: M87 W92R shows no changes in secondary structure or stability compared to wild-type.
source: Indeed, M87 W92R was almost entirely deficient in LL-37 interaction (Figure 4A and B), while showing no changes in secondary structure or stability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by CD data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: M87 Glu85 is the only M87 amino acid seen to make polar contacts in both complexes in the asymmetric unit.
source: The only M87 amino acid seen to make polar contacts in both complexes in the asymmetric unit of the crystal was Glu85 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Alanine substitution of M87 Glu85 has little effect on LL-37 binding.
source: Ala substitution of M87 Glu85 had little effect on LL-37 binding (Figure 4A and B), suggesting that it did not contribute to affinity.
evidence: Supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: M87 Glu85 does not contribute to binding affinity.
source: Ala substitution of M87 Glu85 had little effect on LL-37 binding (Figure 4A and B), suggesting that it did not contribute to affinity.
evidence: Inferred from mutagenesis data

claim: M87 E85R has significantly decreased interaction with LL-37.
source: Consistent with our structural observations and a role in specificity, M87 E85R had significantly decreased interaction with LL-37 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: The decreased LL-37 interaction of M87 E85R is a direct effect, not due to structural changes.
source: This decrease was a direct effect as M87 E85R had greater α-helical content than wild-type M87 protein and similar stability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by CD data showing M87 E85R has greater α-helical content and similar stability

claim: M87 E85R has greater α-helical content than wild-type M87 protein and similar stability.
source: This decrease was a direct effect as M87 E85R had greater α-helical content than wild-type M87 protein and similar stability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by CD data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: M87 a and d heptad position amino acids are important for LL-37 interaction.
source: These results validated the structural observations regarding the mode of interaction between M87 protein and LL-37, and indicated the importance of the M87 a and d heptad position amino acids to the interaction.
evidence: Inferred from mutagenesis results

claim: The polar contact conferred by M87 Glu85 confers specificity rather than binding affinity.
source: They further indicated that the polar contact conferred by M87 Glu85 conferred specificity rather than binding affinity.
evidence: Inferred from mutagenesis results showing E85A has little effect but E85R decreases binding

claim: The molecular weight of intact M87 protein alone is 73.6±1.2 kDa.
source: The molecular weight of intact M87 protein alone was 73.6±1.2 kDa (calc. 72.4 kDa) (Figure 4C, black).
evidence: Supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 4C

claim: When LL-37 is added to M87 protein and immediately analyzed, the complex has a mass of 80.4±0.6 kDa, corresponding to an M87 dimer bound to one or two LL-37 molecules.
source: A 10-fold excess of LL-37 to the intact M87 dimer was added, and the sample was applied to SEC-MALS almost immediately after mixing. The complex had a mass of 80.4±0.6 kDa, which corresponded to an M87 protein dimer bound to one or two molecules of LL-37 (calc. 4.5 kDa) (Figure 4C, blue).
evidence: Supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 4C

claim: After 1 hr of incubation of LL-37 with M87 protein, the mass of the complex is 97.1±0.6 kDa, corresponding to an M87 dimer bound to five or six LL-37 molecules.
source: Notably, after 1 hr of incubation of LL-37 with M87 protein, the mass of the complex was 97.1±0.6 kDa (Figure 4C, red), which corresponded to an M87 protein dimer bound to five or six molecules of LL-37.
evidence: Supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Incubation of LL-37 with M87 protein for up to 4 hr results in the same increased mass as at 1 hr, indicating self-limiting growth of the complex.
source: Incubation of up to 4 hr also resulted in the same increased mass, indicating self-limiting growth of the complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The single LL-37 molecule bound to an M87 dimer can recruit four or five additional LL-37 molecules.
source: These results suggested that the single LL-37 molecule bound to an M87 dimer could recruit four or five additional LL-37 molecules.
evidence: Inferred from SEC-MALS data showing mass increase over time

claim: The wild-type M87 strain is resistant to LL-37.
source: The wild-type M87 strain was resistant to LL-37 (Figure 4D) and indeed had a greater LL-37 MIC than the M1 strain (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by MIC data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The wild-type M87 strain has a greater LL-37 MIC than the M1 strain.
source: The wild-type M87 strain was resistant to LL-37 (Figure 4D) and indeed had a greater LL-37 MIC than the M1 strain (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by MIC data comparing Figure 4D and Figure 1C

claim: Deletion of emm87 leads to significantly increased sensitivity to LL-37.
source: Deletion of emm87 led to significantly increased sensitivity to LL-37 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by MIC data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The Δemm87 strain complemented with wild-type M87 is restored to the LL-37 resistance of the wild-type parental M87 strain.
source: Notably, the Δemm87 strain complemented with wild-type M87 was restored to the LL-37 resistance of the wild-type parental M87 strain, while complemented with M87 E85R remained sensitive to LL-37, similar to the level seen for the uncomplemented Δemm87 strain.
evidence: Supported by MIC data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The Δemm87 strain complemented with M87 E85R remains sensitive to LL-37, similar to the uncomplemented Δemm87 strain.
source: Notably, the Δemm87 strain complemented with wild-type M87 was restored to the LL-37 resistance of the wild-type parental M87 strain, while complemented with M87 E85R remained sensitive to LL-37, similar to the level seen for the uncomplemented Δemm87 strain.
evidence: Supported by MIC data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The LL-37 susceptibility results provide physiological validation for the structural observations.
source: These LL-37 susceptibility results provide physiological validation for our structural observations.
evidence: Inferred from the consistency between structural and functional data

claim: The LL-37-binding motif visualized in M87 protein was identified in the sequence variable N-terminal regions of 14 other M protein types.
source: The LL-37-binding motif visualized in M87 protein was identified in the sequence variable N-terminal regions of 14 other M protein types (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: The LL-37-binding motif consists of two consecutive ideal heptads with a strictly conserved Tyr at the a position of the first heptad.
source: The motif consisted of two consecutive ideal heptads, that is, with a and d positions occupied by canonical hydrophobic amino acids (Wagschal et al., 1999; Tripet et al., 2000; Kwok and Hodges, 2004), including a strictly conserved Tyr at the a position of the first heptad.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and citations

claim: The LL-37-binding motif includes a hydrogen bond acceptor at the e position of the first heptad.
source: Along with these, the motif had a hydrogen bond acceptor at the e position of the first heptad, which in M87 protein (Glu85) provided specificity by contacting LL-37 Lys12 (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and structural data

claim: The LL-37-binding motif excludes a positively charged amino acid from the e position of the second heptad.
source: In addition, a positively charged amino acid was excluded from the e position of the second heptad, which in M87 protein was Trp92 and proximal to LL-37 Arg23 (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and structural data

claim: The LL-37-binding motif is preceded by a nearly ideal heptad with the a position occupied by Leu or Tyr and the d position tolerant of less ideal amino acids like Ala or Gln.
source: Preceding these two ideal heptads was a nearly ideal heptad, with the a position occupied by canonical amino acids (i.e., Leu or Tyr) while the d position was tolerant of less than ideal amino acids (i.e., Ala77 as in M87, and also Gln) (Tripet et al., 2000; Kwok and Hodges, 2004).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and citations

claim: M68N100 binds LL-37.
source: M68N100 bound LL-37 as did M25N100 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: M25N100 binds LL-37.
source: M68N100 bound LL-37 as did M25N100 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: M87N100 E85R has significantly decreased LL-37 binding compared to wild-type M87N100.
source: As the E85R substitution had been evaluated only in intact M87 protein, it was introduced into the M87N100 fragment, which resulted in significantly decreased LL-37 binding as well (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and D

claim: Arg substitution of the equivalent Glu in M25N100 (E87) leads to significantly decreased LL-37 binding.
source: Arg substitution of the equivalent Glu in M25N100 (E87) and M68N100 (E79) also led to significantly decreased LL-37 binding (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and D

claim: Arg substitution of the equivalent Glu in M68N100 (E79) leads to significantly decreased LL-37 binding.
source: Arg substitution of the equivalent Glu in M25N100 (E87) and M68N100 (E79) also led to significantly decreased LL-37 binding (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and D

claim: Arg substitution of M58N100 E97 decreases LL-37 binding, but this effect is not statistically significant.
source: While Arg substitution of M58N100 (E97) decreased LL-37 binding, this effect was not statistically significant.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: M25N100 G82D has significantly higher levels of LL-37 binding compared to wild-type M25N100.
source: In the case of M25 and M58 proteins, we noticed that the amino acid preceding the strictly conserved Tyr was Gly, which is a helix-breaking amino acid. Therefore, we substituted the Gly in M25 and M58 proteins with Asp, which is the equivalent amino acid in M87 (D80), and found that M25N100 G82D and M58N100 G92D had significantly higher levels of LL-37 binding compared to their wild-type counterparts (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: M58N100 G92D has significantly higher levels of LL-37 binding compared to wild-type M58N100.
source: In the case of M25 and M58 proteins, we noticed that the amino acid preceding the strictly conserved Tyr was Gly, which is a helix-breaking amino acid. Therefore, we substituted the Gly in M25 and M58 proteins with Asp, which is the equivalent amino acid in M87 (D80), and found that M25N100 G82D and M58N100 G92D had significantly higher levels of LL-37 binding compared to their wild-type counterparts (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: M25, M58, and M68 bind LL-37 in the same mode as M87 protein.
source: These results are consistent with M25, M58, and M68 binding LL-37 in the same mode as observed for M87 protein and support the hypothesis that the M87 protein LL-37-binding motif is conserved in at least 14 other M proteins, which belong to the E2 or E3 cluster of M proteins (Sanderson-Smith et al., 2014).

claim: The M87 protein LL-37-binding motif is conserved in at least 14 other M proteins belonging to the E2 or E3 cluster.
